questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman requested HPV vaccination. She reported sex with both men and women with five sex partners in the last year. She was tested annually for STIs and HIV . She tested positive for chlamydia 2 years ago and was treated with azithromycin 1 g. All STI tests were negative at her last screening 6 months ago.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Do not vaccinate. Explain that she has likely already been exposed to HPV , and vaccination is not indicated
Do not vaccinate. She is too old to receive the vaccine
Test for presence of HPV using a vaginal swab. If HPV is present, do not vaccinate

questions.explanation: Vaccinate with three-dose series HPV vaccination is recommended for adolescents age 11 or 12 years. Vaccination is also recommended for females between the ages of 13 and 26 and for males between the ages of 13 through 21 who were not adequately vaccinated previously. HPV vaccination is also recommended for gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men, transgender people, and those with some immunocompromising conditions between ages 22 and 26 years, if inadequately vaccinated in the past. The vaccine should be administered regardless of history of exposure.

questions.question: Human papillomavirus (HPV).

parts.text: Oncogenic serotypes.
Papillomatous (wart-causing) serotypes.
Vaccines - serotypes covered, dosage, and indications in males/females.

parts_raw.text: A) Oncogenic serotypes
B) Papillomatous serotypes
C) Vaccines - serotypes, dosage and indicated in males/females.

questions.model_answer:
a) High-risk oncogenic types (IARC): 16, 18, 31, 33, 35, 39, 45, 51, 52, 56, 58, 59, 66. HPV-16 (squamous cell) and HPV-18 (adenocarcinoma) are the most oncogenic and together cause ~70% of cervical cancers; HPV DNA is found in 99.7% of cervical cancers.
b) Anogenital warts (condylomata acuminata) and recurrent respiratory papillomatosis: HPV-6 and HPV-11. Common/plantar/flat cutaneous warts: HPV-1, 2, 3, 4, 27.
c) (1) Cervarix (bivalent) - HPV-16, 18; females. (2) Gardasil (quadrivalent) - HPV-6, 11, 16, 18; males and females. (3) Gardasil 9 (nonavalent) - HPV-6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, 58; males and females. Schedule: 2 doses (0, 6-12 mo) if series started before the 15th birthday; 3 doses (0, 1-2, 6 mo) if started at age 15-26 or if immunocompromised (including HIV).

cohort_answer.text:
16,18 (and others included in HPV 9); 16 & 18 cause 70% of cancers; All 9 serotypes cause 90% of cancers
6,11; Cause 90% of all warts
Bivalent – serotypes 16,18, 2 doses if 9-14, only for females; Quadrivalent – serotypes 6,11,16,18, 2 doses if 9-14, both males and females; HPV-9 – serotypes 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52 and 58, 2 doses 9-14, both males and females; Give vaccines q6mos apart; All immunosuppressed or > 15yo gets 3 doses

questions.question: A man who has sex with men has a partner with anal warts and is himself HIV-positive.
questions.question_raw:
Q28 (2013 PM)
MSM. Patient has partner with anal warts. Patient has HIV.

parts.text: What does HIV do to the risk of genital or anal warts?
Is the HPV vaccine indicated and safe?
How well do condoms reduce the risk of HPV transmission?

parts_raw.text: A. What does HIV do to risk of genital warts or anal warts?
B. Is vaccine indicated or safe?
C. How well do condoms reduce the risk of HPV transmission?

questions.model_answer:
a) HIV increases the incidence and prevalence of genital warts and CIN by 4-fold to 40-fold; risk is greater with low CD4+ counts and high HIV-1 RNA. Risk of invasive anal cancer in MSM is >40-fold increased.
b) Yes - indicated and safe. Gardasil 9 (3-dose schedule) is recommended and the vaccination window extends to age 26 for MSM and immunocompromised/HIV persons; in HIV it is safe, does not affect CD4 count or viral load, though titres are ~30-50% lower.
c) Condoms give imperfect/partial protection. Consistent condom use approximately halves the risk of HPV acquisition in males, and male condom use for >=3 months promotes regression of CIN and penile lesions - not complete protection.
questions.cohort_conflict: Cohort cites ~70% condom protection; the text supports only imperfect/partial protection (consistent use roughly halves acquisition risk in males).

cohort_answer.text:
Increases risk
Yes and safe
70% (50% with HSV, HIV 80%)

questions.question: State two recommendations from NACI regarding the use of HPV vaccination in males.

parts.text: State 2 recommendations from NACI regarding the use of HPV vaccination in males.

parts_raw.text: State 2 recommendations from NACI regarding the use of HPV vaccination in males.

questions.model_answer:
(1) HPV9 is recommended routinely for males 9-26 years of age (routine school-based program at 9-14 years), using the same schedule as females - 2 doses for immunocompetent individuals starting at 9-14 years, 3 doses if starting at 15 years or older.
(2) HPV9 may be given to males 27 years and older, and 3 doses are recommended for immunocompromised males and males who have sex with men regardless of age.
questions.beyond_mandell: NACI HPV vaccine statement (updated recommendations, 9-valent vaccine).
questions.cohort_conflict: Cohort cites quadrivalent vaccine and a 45-year upper age limit; current NACI recommends HPV9, routine for males 9-26, with use permitted at 27 years and older.

cohort_answer.text: Boys now get the quad HPV or HPV-9 the same as girls. Upper age limit: 45yo.

questions.question: What is the only indication for HPV PCR testing of cervical specimens in Canada?

parts.text: State the only indication for HPV PCR testing of cervical specimens in Canada.

parts_raw.text: What is the only indication for HPV PCR testing for cervical specimens in Canada?

questions.model_answer: Triage (reflex testing) of cytology showing atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASC-US) to identify women who require colposcopy. parts_raw.text: For each HPV vaccine type (Bivalent, Quadrivalent), state: serogroups covered, number of doses, and whether licensed for males, females, or both.

questions.model_answer:
Bivalent (Cervarix): HPV types 16 and 18. Doses: 2 doses (0, 6 months) if started at 9-14 years; 3 doses (0, 1, 6 months) if 15 years or older or immunocompromised/HIV. Licensed for females (9-45 years); not licensed for males in Canada.
Quadrivalent (Gardasil): HPV types 6, 11, 16, 18. Doses: 2 doses (0, 6 months) if started at 9-14 years; 3 doses (0, 2, 6 months) if 15 years or older or immunocompromised/HIV. Licensed for both females and males (9-45 years).
For completeness, the 9-valent vaccine (Gardasil 9) adds types 31, 33, 45, 52, 58, uses the same dosing rules, and is licensed for both sexes; it is now the product in use, with bivalent and quadrivalent largely discontinued.
questions.beyond_mandell: NACI HPV statement; bivalent and quadrivalent products have been superseded by HPV9 in Canada.

questions.question: Describe the available HPV vaccines and the HPV types each one covers.

parts.text: Name the HPV vaccines and state the HPV types covered by each.

parts_raw.text: HPV vaccines and coverage

questions.model_answer: Three L1 virus-like-particle (VLP) vaccines have been licensed: (1) Cervarix (GSK) - bivalent, covers HPV-16 and 18; (2) Gardasil (Merck) - quadrivalent, covers HPV-6, 11, 16, 18; (3) Gardasil 9 (Merck) - nonavalent, covers HPV-6, 11, 16, 18 plus the five additional high-risk types 31, 33, 45, 52, 58. All are given IM (0.5 mL, deltoid). Only Gardasil 9 remains available in the US. Two-dose schedule (0, 6-12 mo) if series begun before the 15th birthday; three-dose schedule (0, 1-2, 6 mo) if started at 15-26 yr or if immunocompromised.

cohort_answer.text: CERVARIX (bivalent HPV types 16,18, GSK) (HPV2). GARDASIL (quadrivalent HPV types 6,11,16,18, Merck) (HPV4). GARDASIL9 (nine-valent HPV types 6,11,16,18,31,33,45,52,58, Merck) (HPV9)

questions.question: Human papillomavirus vaccine.

parts.text: Which serotypes are covered by the available human papillomavirus vaccines?
What proportion of cervical cancers are caused by these serotypes?

parts_raw.text: [Serotypes covered by vaccines]
What proportion of cervical CA are caused by these serotypes?

questions.model_answer:
a) Bivalent (Cervarix, HPV2): types 16 and 18. Quadrivalent (Gardasil, HPV4): types 6, 11, 16 and 18. Nonavalent (Gardasil 9, HPV9): types 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52 and 58. Types 6 and 11 are low-risk types causing about 90% of anogenital warts and recurrent respiratory papillomatosis; the remainder are oncogenic.

b) Types 16 and 18 alone account for approximately 70% of cervical cancers. The five additional oncogenic types in the nonavalent vaccine (31, 33, 45, 52, 58) add roughly a further 20%, so the nonavalent vaccine covers approximately 90% of cervical cancers. Bivalent and quadrivalent vaccines therefore cover about 70%.
questions.beyond_mandell: NACI HPV statement; only Gardasil 9 is currently marketed in Canada.

cohort_answer.text: Gardasil (HPV4) quadrivalent: 6, 11, 16, 18. Cervarix (HPV2): 16, 18. Gardasil (HPV9): 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, 58. ~90% of cervical cancers caused by these serotypes (16 and 18 cause ~70%; 31, 33, 45, 52, 58 cause ~20%).

questions.question: A girl with condylomata wants to know about her risk of having an abnormal Pap test.
questions.question_raw:
Q26 (2007)
Girl with condylomata wants to know about her risk of having an abnormal PAP test.

parts.text: What should you tell her?

parts_raw.text: A.  What should you answer her?

questions.model_answer: The presence of external genital warts may indicate coexisting cervical HPV squamous epithelial lesions, including cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN), because both share the same risk factor of sexual HPV transmission and low- and high-risk types often coinfect. She therefore has an increased likelihood of an abnormal Pap and should undergo cervical cytologic screening; because morphologic differentiation of lesion grade is unreliable, biopsy is recommended for any suspicious cervical finding.

cohort_answer.text: The presence of external genital warts may indicate the existence of cervical HPV squamous epithelial lesions, including CIN bc common risk factor (sexual activity)

questions.question: Regarding HPV.

parts.text: Describe the methods of detection/diagnosis of HPV infection.

parts_raw.text: B. Method of detection

questions.model_answer: (1) Clinical/physical examination - exophytic warts have a characteristic appearance; colposcopy or nasal speculum with 3-5% acetic acid application reveals acetowhite subclinical lesions (also high-resolution anoscopy for anal disease). (2) Cytology - the Papanicolaou (Pap) smear, koilocytes are the histologic hallmark; classified by the Bethesda system (ASC-US/ASC-H, LSIL, HSIL, SCC). (3) Histology/biopsy - the gold standard, confirms diagnosis and identifies intraepithelial neoplasia or invasive cancer; p16INK4A immunohistochemistry is an adjunct prognostic marker. (4) HPV nucleic acid detection (FDA-approved) - e.g. Hybrid Capture II, Cervista HPV HR/16-18, COBAS 4800 (only one approved for primary screening), APTIMA, ONCLARITY; used for primary screening, reflex testing of ASC-US, and co-testing with cytology in women >=30 yr. Virus culture is not available and serology is not used for clinical diagnosis (insufficient sensitivity/specificity).

cohort_answer.text: *Male anal paps guideline? Initiate screening with Pap (cytology) at age 21 (or 25) if any Hx of any sexual activity. Every 3 years if no abnormality. Same for pregnancy, WSW, HPV-vaccinated, subtotal-hysterectomy, transgender men. Annual testing for Hx of HSIL, cervical cancer, HIV+ or immunosuppressed. Discontinue at 70 yo if 3 or more negative cytology in previous 10 years. No routine HPV immunohistochemical testing -> only if abnormality on cytology (vs American guidelines)

questions.question: Name 6 different viruses and an associated malignancy with each one.

parts.text: Name 6 different viruses and an associated malignancy with each one.

parts_raw.text: Name 6 different viruses and an associated malignancy with each one

questions.model_answer: (1) Epstein-Barr virus (HHV-4) - Burkitt lymphoma / nasopharyngeal carcinoma. (2) Human herpesvirus 8 (KSHV) - Kaposi sarcoma / primary effusion lymphoma. (3) Human papillomavirus (high-risk, e.g. 16/18) - cervical and oropharyngeal carcinoma. (4) Hepatitis B virus - hepatocellular carcinoma. (5) Hepatitis C virus - hepatocellular carcinoma. (6) Human T-lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1) - adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma.
questions.beyond_mandell: Cross-virus oncogenic associations (HPV, HBV, HCV, HTLV-1, HHV-8) are established knowledge/IARC classification; only EBV and HHV-8 are covered in this chapter.
